questions.stem: How many electrons do Group 1 elements have in their outer shell?
questions.explanation: All Group 1 elements have 1 electron in their outer shell. This single outer electron is easily lost during reactions, making them highly reactive metals.

questions.stem: What happens to the reactivity of Group 1 metals as you go down the group?
questions.explanation: Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is more easily lost. There are more inner electron shells shielding the outer electron from the nuclear charge.

questions.stem: What are the products when lithium reacts with water?
questions.explanation: Lithium reacts with water to produce lithium hydroxide (an alkaline solution) and hydrogen gas: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂.

questions.stem: Why are Group 1 metals stored in oil?

options.text: To prevent them from reacting with oxygen and moisture in the air

questions.explanation: Group 1 metals are so reactive that they react quickly with oxygen and water vapour in the air. Storing them under oil prevents contact with air and moisture.

questions.stem: Which Group 1 metal reacts most vigorously with water?

options.text: All react at the same rate

questions.explanation: Potassium reacts most vigorously because it is furthest down the group of the three. It burns with a lilac flame on water and may even ignite the hydrogen gas produced.

questions.stem: What type of ion do Group 1 elements form when they react?
questions.explanation: Group 1 elements lose their single outer electron to form 1+ ions (e.g., Na⁺, K⁺). This gives them a stable full outer shell electronic configuration.

questions.stem: Which physical property is unusual for Group 1 metals compared to most other metals?

options.text: They are soft enough to cut with a knife and have low densities
They are solid at room temperature
They are shiny when freshly cut

questions.explanation: Unlike most metals, Group 1 elements are very soft (can be cut with a knife) and have low densities. Lithium, sodium, and potassium are less dense than water.
